findings.summary: Criterion 3 asks for N./N)/(N) numbered parts. The plan covers `1.`, `1)` and `(a)`, but has no `(1)` case and no `(1)` entry in the form list.
findings.evidence: Criterion 3: 'N./N)/(N) numbered parts'. The plan's cases (2) to (4) are `1.`/`2.`/`3.`, `1)` and `(a)(b)(c)`. Decision 4's form list is: dash, star, `1.`, `1)`, `(a)`, request citing a job, retry complaint, governance path, crate-relative path. Fix: Add a `(1)(2)(3)` case that pins 0 bullets, labeled as a known gap like the `1)` case. Add `(1)` to the form list that corpus_covers_the_listed_input_forms checks. Keep `(a)` as well.
findings.location: Demonstrations, criterion 3, and Decision 4 (fixed list of input forms)

findings.summary: Several expected outcomes were predicted by reasoning, not by running the gate. That is the same fault this job removes. The plan does not say what the producer should do when the gate returns something else.
findings.evidence: Case 14 expects that `GitHub/env-var` and `owner/repo` are accepted by check_reading_references. Case 6 relies on followed_up_ids matching 'Follow up on job <id>'. Neither was checked against the matching code (the matching logic of followed_up_ids and check_reading_references was not read). Changing any check body is out of scope (criterion 6, 'Touch no check body'). Fix: Tell the producer to pin whatever the gate returns today. When a real shape gets the wrong outcome, the producer labels it a known gap in the case (as the `1)` case is labeled) and names it as a follow-up. The producer must not change a check to make a case pass, and must not quietly drop the case.
findings.location: Demonstrations, criterion 3, cases 5, 6 and 14; Steps 3 and 8

findings.summary: A new refusal rule added inside an existing check_* function needs no new corpus case under the mechanism. This is probably the most common way a rule gets changed.
findings.evidence: The extractor matches only `step!(check_*(` lines inside refusing_check. The plan states this limit for the parser and stems, but not for new branches inside existing checks. Fix: Name this case in the stated limit: in the test header, CHANGELOG and decisions entry, and in the planner rule ('a change to an existing check adds a refusing case for the new branch').

summary: I checked the plan against the code by reading it; I ran nothing. Every code claim I checked holds. check_reading_acceptance (reading.rs:3013-3026) runs the six named checks in the stated order, and the first one takes continued_jobs(request, attempt, referenced). All six checks, continued_jobs and request_text_acceptance are pub, and `reading` is a pub module, so an integration test can reach the real gate. is_bullet (2239) matches only `- `, `* ` and digits followed by `. `, so the pinned counts of 0 for `1)` and `(a)` are right. continued_jobs leaves out jobs the request only cites, so corpus case 5 (accepted) fits today's code. The 500-token frame cap is at lib.rs:402. planner_brief has a `## Report` section (briefs.rs:1347) next to the existing seam test at 2081. reading.rs's own tests already split the source text on function names (6228, 7918), so a source-scanning test has precedent. The design is sound. It fixes the problem at the shared gate (refusing_check built by a step! macro using stringify!, so no hand-kept list of check names can drift). It adds a stored corpus with labeled sources and a mechanism test that requires a refusing case for every check step. It words the planner rule honestly for a planner that can only Read, Grep and Glob, and it says plainly that the mechanism does not cover parser, stem and stop-list changes. The demonstrations name real seams, call no doubles, and would fail without the change. What remains is minor: one input form named in criterion 3 has no case, and the plan does not say what the producer should do when a case's predicted outcome does not match what the gate actually returns.
